newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS-U.S.and EU trumpet breakthrough on trade.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-U.S.and EU trumpet breakthrough on trade.

text.p: The United States and the European Union said on Wednesday they had cleared the way for a deal allowing their businesses once-for-all safety standards approval in five product categories worth $40 billion a year.

"We feel that we have a breakthrough and we hope that it will lead to an agreement in the next few days," U.S. President Bill Clinton said after EU-U.S. talks with Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok and European Commission President Jacques Santer.
The two sides also signed a cooperation accord on controlling chemicals used to make synthetic drugs and a customs deal Kok said would boost trade and help fight fraud and graft.
He said the two sides had also cracked bilateral differences on animal inspections, preventing a possible transatlantic row on meat quality standards.
"We also reached an agreement on veterinary inspection, thus resolving a trade conflict that might otherwise have arisen on the export of meat products," Kok said.
While the customs cooperation and drugs precursors deals were flagged well in advance of Wednesday's summit, the one on so-called Mutual Recognition Agreements (MRAs) came as more of a surprise.
Both Kok and Santer echoed Clinton's assessment of an MRA deal being but a few days away but European Commission officials warned that any text still had to go to EU capitals.
MRAs are expected to cut manufacturers' marketing costs by as much as 10 percent by allowing each party to recognise the other's testing, inspection and certification procedures.
A U.S. official said ahead of the set-piece talks that MRAs on product standards had been sorted within the final hours.
The official said MRAs would reduce marketing costs for telecommunications equipment, information-technology products, pharmaceuticals, medical devices and pleasure boats.
Final sticking points concerned U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulation of pharmaceuticals and medical devices.

He said the FDA was legally prohibited from ceding final inspection authority over the manufacturing of these devices, but as a practical matter would "not feel the need to do so" in the case of already-approved products manufactured under EU standards.
